caseRecord.summary: An elderly customer received an SMS appearing in the same thread as her usual bank messages, warning of a suspicious login and directing her to call a number or visit a link. She called the number, and a man claiming to be from the bank's fraud team guided her through logging in on a page he provided and had her read back an SMS code. A transfer to a so-called safe account followed. The caller is reportedly still contacting her and asking for another code.

Ongoing contact from the scammer, who is requesting another one-time code

recommendedNextSteps: Advise the customer immediately not to share any further codes, not to log in via any link or page provided by the caller, and to end the call [BK-G1]
Flag the case to the fraud team now and request a hold on the transfer and the account; the AI does not initiate the hold [BK-G1]
Ask the fraud team to confirm whether the scammer's session or access to online banking remains active [BK-G2]
Reset the online banking password and access PIN through official bank channels, not through any link or number provided by the caller [BK-G2]
Consider card re-issue and confirm whether card details or PINs were also disclosed, since the handover lists only login details and an SMS code [BK-G2]

Establish the transfer timestamp and whether the destination account is domestic, then raise a recall request with the fraud team; recovery likelihood drops after 24 hours but the request should still be raised [BK-G3]
Refer the customer to the financial-hardship team and the identity-recovery/victim-support partner given distress, age, isolation and a large loss [BK-G5]

Check with the customer whether she has been asked to pay any 'fees' to release funds, as a second-wave indicator, although guidance BK-G4 is written for investment and romance scams and applies only by analogy [BK-G4]

assessment.scamSummary: Suspected bank-impersonation scam: an SMS in the customer's usual bank thread led to a call with someone claiming to be the bank's fraud team, a login on a page the caller supplied, and a one-time code read out. A suspected AUD 4,200 transfer to a so-called 'safe account' followed, and the caller is reportedly still pressing for another code.
assessment.priorityRationale: The incident is ongoing, a transfer has reportedly been completed, login details and a one-time code were disclosed, and the caller is asking for another code. The customer is elderly, distressed and isolated.

recommendedActions.action: Tell the customer now to stop speaking to the caller, not to read out or share any further codes, and not to use any link or page the caller or SMS gave her [BK-G1].
Escalate to the fraud team immediately and request a hold on the transfer and on the account. The AI does not initiate holds; the employee can escalate this [BK-G1].
Ask the fraud team to check whether the scammer's online banking session or access is still active, and to review recovery details and registered devices for changes [BK-G2, DP-G2].

Arrange a password and access PIN reset through official bank channels only, never via the caller's link or number. Confirm the timing with the fraud team so it fits with their containment steps [BK-G2, DP-G2].

Ask whether the caller asked her to install software or share her screen. If yes, advise disconnecting the device from the internet and refer it to the digital-platform/IT partner before any further banking use [TL-G4].

Ask whether she has lost mobile service or received porting or SIM-change messages. If yes, treat it as a possible SIM swap and urgently contact her carrier for a port-out lock and account-change check [TL-G2].
Confirm whether her card number or PIN was disclosed, and consider a card re-issue [BK-G2].
Ask whether the same password is used on other accounts such as email, and reset those too if so [DP-G2].

Establish the transfer time, source account and destination details, then ask the fraud team to raise a recall request. Recovery chances drop after 24 hours, but the request should still be raised [BK-G3].
Record exactly the SMS sender ID, 0400 000 000 and any further numbers used. Lodge the numbers with the telco scam-reporting channel for blocking assessment; the AI does not block numbers [TL-G1].
Record examplebank-secure.example exactly and submit it to the host/platform abuse channel for takedown assessment [DP-G1].
Ask the customer to keep the SMS thread, call log and any screenshots as evidence, and to report any further calls or texts [DP-G3, TL-G1].
Ask whether she has been told to pay any 'fees' to release funds, as a possible second-wave sign. BK-G4 is written for investment and romance scams, so this applies by analogy only [BK-G4].
Make the referrals listed below, including support for the customer.

The transfer time, source account, destination details and method (customer-initiated or caller-initiated) are unknown.
It is unknown whether the customer is on the phone with the caller right now, or has given further codes since the transfer.
It is unknown whether card details, remote access or SIM-swap activity were involved.
The SMS sender ID and the exact login page URL are not recorded, and it is unclear whether the page URL differs from the SMS link.

Sender spoofing is inferred from the SMS appearing in the bank thread, not confirmed.
The customer's isolation and distress raise the risk of further manipulation.
itemsRequiringHumanReview: All three specialists (banking, telecom, digital platform) reported medium confidence, so every recommendation needs employee or fraud-team judgement.

Banking and digital platform say the scammer's phone number or URL is not recorded, but the case record lists 0400 000 000 and examplebank-secure.example. Please verify these against the original report.
No guidance covers bank impersonation through a spoofed SMS thread or phone-based impersonation, so related steps rest on analogy.
The digital platform agent notes there is no guidance on refusing caller-requested codes. Confirm the frontline script with the team.
Banking suggests a financial-hardship team referral, but hardship is not stated (only that the customer receives a pension). Confirm whether it is appropriate.
The digital platform agent suggests enabling two-factor authentication, but an SMS code is already in use. Confirm with the fraud team which controls to apply.
Confirm the order of the password reset and the fraud team's session review, so that evidence and containment are not undermined.
BK-G4 on 'fees' applies only by analogy to this scam pattern.
Whether law enforcement reporting is required depends on the organisation's policy and needs confirming.
Decide who contacts the carrier and the host abuse channel, as these are not in the referral directory.
assessment.suggestedCommunicationToAffectedPerson: Thank you for telling us. You have done the right thing. Please don't share any more codes with the caller, and please hang up if they ring again. A message sitting in your bank's usual thread doesn't prove it came from the bank, so we'd like to check this together. We're asking our fraud team to look at your account right away, and we'll reset your password through our official channels. Could you tell me roughly when the transfer happened, and whether you gave out your card number? None of this is your fault; these callers are very convincing. We can also connect you with people who can support you, if you'd like.
